Variable-height lazy stack rows are implemented and committed.

**What changed**
- Protocol: `ITEM_EXTENTS` (`0x0025`, LIST), `FIRST_ITEM_OFFSET` (`0x0026`, F32), `TOTAL_EXTENT` (`0x0027`, F32); manifest + Java/TS constants regenerated.
- Kotlin: `ForEach(items, itemExtents = listOf(...))`; the lazy stack emits the window extents/offset/total, sets each row’s main-axis size from its extent, and keeps `ITEM_EXTENT` as the average/default. Lazy grids remain uniform.
- HTML (Rust + Java): variable-extent padding and `data-pathland-item-extents` / `-first-item-offset` / `-total-extent`.
- DOM client: variable-extent virtual padding and visible-range mapping.
- GTK/Qt: variable-extent spacer sizes and range math for lazy stacks.
- Spec (`LAYOUT`, `PRIMITIVES`, `MODIFIERS`, `DSL`) and statuses updated.

**Verified**
- Kotlin `DslTest#lazyStackSupportsVariableItemExtents`.
- Rust/Java HTML variable-extent tests.
- Full `cargo test`, `mvn -P jvm-only test`, and TS typecheck + 297 tests green.
- Engine trace `--check` current; working tree clean at `9ff7c1c9`.

**Remaining**
- Keyed row-local state across eviction + focused-row pinning.
- Rust DSL variable extents (`ForEach` currently exposes only `item_extent`).
- Rust DSL lazy grids.
- Keyed window reconcile for the build-time Rust engine + a shared slide trace.
- Qt lazy-grid app padding; HTML C22/C24 tests.

## Objective
- Implement variable-height rows for the lazy stack/grid virtualization work (app-declared per-item extents) after completing lazy stacks/grids and the 1000-row MusicPlayer demo.

## Important Details
- Branch: `feat/lazy-stack-virtualization`; last commit `ba60c943` (demo status). Variable-height work is currently uncommitted.
- v1 variable-height model: **app-declared per-item extents**; no renderer measurement yet. Grids explicitly reject `itemExtents` (`check(data.itemExtents == null)`).
- New protocol properties: `ITEM_EXTENTS 0x0025` (LIST F32, emitted window extents), `FIRST_ITEM_OFFSET 0x0026` (F32), `TOTAL_EXTENT 0x0027` (F32). `ITEM_EXTENT` remains the fixed/average fallback.
- Kotlin `LazyStackView` computes `firstOffset`/`totalExtent` with O(N) loops, emits the three properties, and forces each row’s `HEIGHT`/`WIDTH` to its extent (removes the property binding).
- Demo decisions locked earlier: 1000 repeated tracks, playlist traverses all 1000, album count repeats 1000, rows are tappable `HStack`s at fixed 64 pt (`LIBRARY_ROW_HEIGHT`). Variable-height is not yet used by the demo.
- Protocol manifest regenerated; TS constants regenerated.

## Work State
### Completed
- Lazy stacks/grids implemented across JVM, Rust, HTML/DOM, GTK, Qt; demo renders a 1000-row lazy list (commits `e135e62c` … `ba60c943`).
- Variable-height protocol surface: Rust `constants.rs`, Java `Properties`/`ValueTypes`, TS codegen, `spec/protocol.tsv` regenerated.
- Kotlin: `ForEachView.itemExtents`; `ForEach(...)` overloads accept `itemExtents: List<Float>?`; `LazyStackView` variable extents; `LazyGridWindowView` rejects extents. `DslTest#lazyStackSupportsVariableItemExtents` passes.

- GTK: `LazyInfo` (no longer `Copy`) gains `extents`, `first_offset`, `total_extent`; `report_lazy_range` and `sync_lazy_stack` updated; `cargo check -p pathland-render-gtk` passes.

There is a bug in the track list in the browser: ## Bug
CSS `-webkit-line-clamp` does not take effect on track entries rendered by the web DOM client. The visible symptom is that track titles/artists in the 1000-row lazy music library are clipped or wrapped instead of ending with an ellipsis. SSR-rendered rows behave correctly, but rows created/recycled by the client after scrolling do not.

## Root cause
`lib/typescript/src/classes.ts`, in the `PROP_LINE_LIMIT` handler around lines 347-364, sets:

    (el.style as unknown as Record<string, string>).boxOrient = "vertical";

`box-orient` is not implemented by browsers for this use; the CSSOM assignment is effectively a no-op. Browsers require the prefixed property `-webkit-box-orient: vertical` for legacy `-webkit-line-clamp` to work. As a result, client-rendered nodes get `display:-webkit-box`, `-webkit-line-clamp`, and `overflow:hidden`, but horizontal box orientation, so the clamp is ignored.

This is why the initial SSR rows work: `lib/java/pathland-render-html/src/main/java/dev/pathland/render/html/HtmlRenderer.java:530` correctly emits `-webkit-box-orient:vertical`. The bug is only in the TypeScript client path, which is used for lazy-list rows and property updates.

Verified in Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox: setting only `style.boxOrient = "vertical"` leaves computed `-webkit-box-orient` as `horizontal` and the text unclamped; setting `-webkit-box-orient` clamps correctly.

## Fix
1. In `lib/typescript/src/classes.ts`, change the `PROP_LINE_LIMIT` handler to use the prefixed property through `setProperty`/`removeProperty`, for example:

    if (n > 0) {
      el.style.display = "-webkit-box";
      el.style.webkitLineClamp = String(n);
      el.style.setProperty("-webkit-box-orient", "vertical");
      el.style.overflow = "hidden";
    } else {
      el.style.webkitLineClamp = "";
      el.style.removeProperty("-webkit-box-orient");
      el.style.overflow = "";
      if (el.style.display === "-webkit-box") {
        el.style.display = "";
      }
    }

   Keep the existing behavior of restoring `display` and clearing all clamp-related properties on reset. Do not change the Java HTML renderer; it is already correct.

2. Update the tests that currently mask the bug:
   - `lib/typescript/test/apply.test.ts` around line 934 currently asserts `boxOrient === "vertical"`. Change it to assert `span.style.getPropertyValue("-webkit-box-orient") === "vertical"`, and ideally also assert the computed/serialized value.
   - `lib/typescript/test/classes.test.ts` around line 82 should assert `el.style.getPropertyValue("-webkit-box-orient") === "vertical"` after a positive limit, and `""` after reset.
   - Add a guard that would fail if the implementation only sets the unprefixed `box-orient` property.
   - Note: happy-dom drops `display:-webkit-box`, so do not try to assert the display value in happy-dom. `getPropertyValue("-webkit-box-orient")` works in happy-dom.

3. Update `lib/typescript/status.md` where it describes `LINE_LIMIT` (around line 52) so the documented implementation explicitly says it sets `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`.

4. Regenerate the shipped bundles. Do not hand-edit generated files. Run:

    npm --prefix lib/typescript run build:all

   This runs typecheck, builds `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js`, and copies it into:
   - `lib/java/pathland-quarkus/src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/_pathland/`
   - `lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/src/main/resources/static/_pathland/`
   It prunes stale hashed bundles and updates `dom-renderer.current`. Inspect `git status` to confirm the new hashed file and manifest are present and stale bundles are removed. Do not commit unless explicitly asked.

5. Run the client tests:

    npm --prefix lib/typescript test

## Verification
The Quarkus dev server currently returns HTTP 500 from an unrelated stale dev-mode class error (`NoSuchMethodError ... ForEach$default`). Restart it cleanly using the documented command:

    cd /Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo && mvn quarkus:dev

Do not work around the 500 by changing application code; it is a stale-process/build issue.

Then verify against http://localhost:8080:
- Initial SSR track rows still clamp to one line with an ellipsis.
- Scroll the library far enough to force the lazy list to create new rows. For client-created rows, check that `getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue("-webkit-box-orient")` is `vertical`, `getComputedStyle(el).webkitLineClamp` is `1`, and clamping is active (`clientHeight < scrollHeight`).
- Use a narrow viewport (for example 360px wide) or another width where the subtitle text exceeds its container, so the clamp actually has to do work. The track title/artist spans are the elements with the clamp; the library row itself is a flex container and is not the clamp target.
- If possible, repeat in Chromium and WebKit. Playwright browsers may already be cached in `~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright`; do not add new dependencies unless necessary.

## Acceptance criteria
- Client-rendered and SSR-rendered track entries behave identically: one-line clamp with an ellipsis when text overflows.
- The generated DOM bundle contains the prefixed `-webkit-box-orient` assignment and no longer relies on unprefixed `boxOrient` for line clamping.
- `npm --prefix lib/typescript test` passes.
- Typecheck/build succeeds and the generated hashed bundles/manifests are consistent.
- No changes are made to Kotlin track views; they already request `.lineLimit(1)`. The defect is renderer-level.

name: pathland-orient
description: Assemble the governing Pathland specs, ADRs, source references, tests, and implementation gaps before a substantial coding task. Read-only and scoped to the requested change.
---

# Pathland orientation

## Trigger

Before substantial work on a Pathland subsystem, or when asked to identify the
constraints governing a file or proposed change. Accept a path, subsystem, or
task description. With no scope, inspect current staged/unstaged changes and
non-ignored untracked files; if none identify a task, ask rather than audit the
whole repository.

## Invariants

- Read-only: do not edit files, install tools, or change branches.
- Follow [document responsibilities](../../../docs/decisions/README.md) and
  [traceability policy](../../../docs/decisions/traceability.md). Specs define
  current requirements; ADRs explain decisions; `status.md` records coverage.
- Read actual target sections, not just filenames, reference glosses, or the ADR
  index. Proposed/Rejected/Superseded ADRs are not accepted current constraints.
- Cite evidence. Do not infer undocumented intent, certify implementation from
  a valid link, or silently choose a winner when documents conflict.
- Do not spawn agents or send code to another provider as part of orientation.

## Workflow

1. Locate the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) and relevant
   `AGENTS.md` instructions. Paths in prose below are repository-root-relative;
   Markdown links in this skill are relative to its own directory.
2. Determine the exact scope. Read `docs/decisions/README.md`, the relevant
   specs, and affected projects' `status.md`. Search the index and source even
   when no `@ref` exists; unannotated code is not necessarily unconstrained.
3. Follow standalone source `@ref` targets in scope, resolving paths from the
   repository root. Read linked ADR rationale and follow supersession links.
   Broaden one hop to related contracts/tests only when relevant to the task.
4. Inspect implementation entry points and existing tests. Find known issues
   in linked audit reports; distinguish a dated audit from current coverage.
5. Report broken references, contradictory contracts, and unexplained choices
   as open questions. Do not repair them during orientation.

## Artifact

Return a compact context pack in the conversation:

- Scope and affected projects.
- Governing spec sections and accepted ADRs, with links and a short explanation.
- Key constraints, each tied to a source; relevant rationale kept distinct.
- Existing tests, known gaps, and any unresolved drift or uncertainty.
- Likely spec/ADR/status/reference updates if the proposed change lands.
- Suggested hand-off, if any. Do not create a context or plan file by default.

## Hand-offs

- A new architectural choice is needed: `pathland-decision`.
- A proposal needs evaluation: `pathland-review`.
- Broken references or suspected code/doc disagreement: `pathland-maintain`.
- Otherwise return to the requested coding task; orientation itself makes no changes.

### 4.4 Gestures

| Gesture | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Kotlin DSL | Rust DSL |
|---------|---------------------------|----------|----------|
| tap | `.onTapGesture { action }` | `.modifiers(tapGesture(g -> g.action(Runnable)))` | `.modifiers(TapGesture::new(f))` |
| raw pointer | `.gesture` composition from raw inputs | `.modifiers(pointerEvents(p -> p.mask(int)))` | `.pointer_events(u32 mask)` |

Tap is **not** a protocol event: it is composed app-side from `POINTER_DOWN`
then `POINTER_UP` on the same target (`EVENT_LISTENERS` bits 0|2). The
`TapGesture` modifier value declares those listeners and records the action;
the host routes the recognized tap via the emitter's tap-action registry.

### 4.5 Navigation

Navigation is **reactive structure over a route signal**
([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)): a
`NavigationContainer` is a component whose tracked render selects the current
route-table destination. The wire surface is minimal and entirely optional:
`ROUTE` (MODIFIERS.md `0x2019`, a STRING current-path property on the slot),
`NAV_DEPTH` (MODIFIERS.md `0x201A`, a U32 back-stack-depth property on the
slot), `NAV_CHROME` (MODIFIERS.md `0x201B`, an F32-enum chrome-mode property
on the slot), `TRANSITION` (MODIFIERS.md `0x1031`, a presentation hint), and
the `NAVIGATE` event (EVENTS.md `0x0E`, host→guest). Renderers stay
stateless: they render whatever destination subtree the app emits and **may**
animate a swap when the `TRANSITION` hint is present, but must render normally
when they ignore it.

**Navigation is opt-in — the developer declares it by inserting a
`NavigationContainer`.** A tree without one has no navigation and the renderer
adds none. The container's chrome mode decides who supplies the navigation UI:

- `PlatformDefault` (default): the **renderer** supplies the chrome — the
  platform's native navigation container where one exists, and a renderer-drawn
  back affordance where none exists.
  `NavigationContainer.make(n -> n.router(router))`.
- `Custom`: the **developer owns all navigation UI** — they draw their own
  back buttons / bars in the destinations and call `router.back()` /
  `navigate(...)` directly; the renderer adds no chrome (no native header-bar
  back button, no DOM back button).
  `NavigationContainer.make(n -> n.router(router).chrome(Chrome.CUSTOM))`.
  Renderers treat a missing `NAV_CHROME` as `PlatformDefault`.

| View | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Kotlin DSL | Rust DSL | Emits / Binds |
|------|----------------------------|----------|----------|---------------|
| `NavigationContainer` | `NavigationStack(path:) { destination(for:) }` | `NavigationContainer.make(n -> n.router(Router).chrome(Chrome))` | `NavigationContainer::with(|n| n.router(router))` | a `Group` slot + `ROUTE` `0x2019`, `NAV_DEPTH` `0x201A`, `NAV_CHROME` `0x201B`, `TRANSITION` `0x1031`; destination swap = `TREE` deltas |
| `NavigationLink` | `NavigationLink("label", value:)` | `NavigationLink.make(l -> l.label(String).router(Router).to(String))` / `NavigationLink.make(l -> l.label(String).to(String))` (router-agnostic) | `navigation_link(...)` | a `BUTTON` whose tap pushes `to` (via the router, or resolved to the nearest enclosing router when router-agnostic) |
| `RouteTable` | — | `RouteTable` (builder), or `Navigation.navigator(...)` (the ergonomic facade) | `RouteTable::new(...)` | none (app-side matching) |

**Router state** — app-owned (never renderer state):

- `Route` = absolute path + path params (`/users/:id` → `{id:"42"}`) + query.
  Path params are strings; typed params are a DSL concern.
- `RouteTable` maps path patterns to destination factories, captures params,
  and runs **guards**; a guard redirects via `replace()`. Factories are lazy —
  in the SSR model the client only ever receives the chosen destination's
  deltas.
- `Router` owns a `Signal<Route>` plus a **back-stack** and exposes
  `navigate` / `push` / `pop` / `replace` / `back`. `push` appends; `pop` /
  `back` step back; `navigate` / `replace` set the current route. The current
  path is emitted as the `ROUTE` property on the container slot.
- The route is a **plain signal — not persisted**. On the web the URL is the
  persistence layer (the DOM client mirrors it via `pushState`/`popstate`); on
  native the route is per-session.
- The initial route is delivered as a **`META::ENVIRONMENT` `ROUTE` field**
  (host → guest platform environment, OPCODE.md — the same message that carries
  the viewport): on SSR the host synthesizes it from the HTTP request (the
  request path — all the request offers), and over the WebSocket the DOM client
  sends it (with the viewport) as its **first** message; a reconnect re-sends it.
  The application applies the environment
  uniformly — the router hydrates from the `ROUTE` field before mount, so a
  deep-link request renders the right destination on the first frame. The app
  never models the platform's location handling — history adaptation
  (`pushState` / `replaceState` / back) is a renderer/DOM-client translation of
  the `ROUTE` property and the `NAVIGATE` event.

**Reserved framework root** — the host reserves **`/_pathland/**`** for its own
system endpoints, so app routes never collide with them: the WebSocket lives at
`/_pathland/ws`, the DOM-client bundle under a **content-hashed name**
(`/_pathland/dom-renderer-<sha256>.js`; the current name is published next to the
copies in the pointer `/_pathland/dom-renderer.current` (name + SRI digest), read by the SSR
layer so the page always references the built artifact — the fresh URL per build
busts immutable asset caches), the
renderer-owned icon glyphs at `/_pathland/icons/<name>.svg` (served from the
shared HTML-renderer library — `pathland_html_icon_svg` over the C ABI — which
the DOM client lazily fetches when a delta references an `ICON_NAME` the page
did not embed), and the host's asset mount at `/_pathland/assets/**`. App routes
are everything else (served by the SSR catch-all). The DOM client reads the
base from the SSR page's `data-pathland-base` attribute (default `/_pathland`),
so a host can relocate it behind a proxy. Asset references in the UI model are
**absolute** (`/_pathland/assets/icons/home.svg`) so deep-linked routes resolve
correctly.

**The `Navigation` facade** — the ergonomic entry point. `Navigation.navigator`
collapses the route table + router + seeding into one readable flow, and
`Navigation.container(router)` is the container:

```java
Router router = Navigation.navigator("/kitchen")     // seeds the initial path
    .route("/",          new HomeView())             // View overload (no params)
    .route("/users/:id", params -> new UserView(params.intValue("id")))
    .fallback(new NotFoundView())

#### Virtualized lists (`LazyVStack` / `LazyHStack`)

A `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack` containing a `ForEach` is a **windowed data
container**. The app supplies the collection and the row builder; the engine
owns the window and evaluates the builder only for visible rows:

```kotlin
LazyVStack(spacing = 0) {
    ForEach(items) { item, _ ->
        RowView(item)
            .frame(height = 44f)   // fixed main-axis extent
    }
}
```

Rules:

- `ForEach` inside a lazy stack is a **data source**, not an eager child list.
  Outside a lazy stack it keeps its eager behavior.
- The lazy stack's content MUST be exactly one `ForEach` for virtualization;
  other children keep the eager stack behavior.
- `ITEM_COUNT` = the collection size. `ITEM_EXTENT` = the row's fixed main-axis
  size, read from the first realized row's `HEIGHT` (VStack) / `WIDTH` (HStack).
  If the row has no fixed main-axis frame, the author MUST pass an explicit
  `itemExtent` (e.g. `ForEach(items, itemExtent = 44f)`); otherwise the DSL
  reports an authoring error. Every row MUST use the same extent.
- Variable heights: `ForEach(items, itemExtents = listOf(44f, 60f, …))` supplies
  one main-axis extent per item. The engine emits `ITEM_EXTENTS` for the window,
  `FIRST_ITEM_OFFSET`, and `TOTAL_EXTENT`; `ITEM_EXTENT` remains the default
  estimate for items outside the window. Lazy grids use a uniform extent.
- `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` = the window start. The engine sets it; the author does not.
- The DSL sets `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit 10 (`VISIBLE_RANGE`) and routes the event
  to the engine's internal window; the author does not manage a window signal.
- The engine reconciles window children by absolute index, or by an optional
  `key` extractor (`ForEach(items, key = { it.id })`); without a key, identity
  is the absolute index.
- Row-local component state is not preserved after a row leaves the window; keep
  row state in the data model (keyed state is a follow-up).
- A full-snapshot/SSR emission carries the first window plus the full virtual
  extent; the client corrects the window after `META::ENVIRONMENT`.
- `LazyVGrid`/`LazyHGrid` use the same data-source window with a **row** or
  **column** unit: `ITEM_COUNT` is the row/column count, `ITEM_EXTENT` the row
  height/column width, and `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` the first visible row/column. The
  emitted children are the cells of the visible units (row-major for VGrid,
  column-major for HGrid). The grid's `columns`/`rows` (or `GRID_TRACKS`)
  define the cells per unit.

The window math, child placement, and visible-range derivation are specified in
[LAYOUT.md §Virtual extent](./LAYOUT.md#virtual-extent-lazy-containers). The
decision and rationale are in
[ADR-0014](../docs/decisions/0014-virtualized-lazy-stacks.md).

### 4.3 Semantic controls

Two-way value controls bind a `WritableSignal` (a config value). Actions bind a
callback. Controls marked **content-bearing** expose `children(...)` for their
content (their style turns it into the control's child, [§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).

| Control | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Kotlin DSL | Emits / Binds |
|---------|---------------------------|----------|---------------|
| `Button` | `Button("title", action)` / `Button(action:label:)` | **content-bearing** — `Button.make(b -> b.title(String).action(Runnable))` and/or `.children(View)`; the title string is handed to the active `ButtonStyle`, an explicit child takes precedence ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)) | `BUTTON` 0x20 (control node); tap = composed `POINTER_DOWN`+`POINTER_UP` |
| `TextField` | `TextField("placeholder", text: writable)` | `TextField.make(t -> t.placeholder(String).text(WritableSignal<String>))` | `TEXT_FIELD` 0x21; `TEXT_CHANGED` → text input |
| `SecureField` | `SecureField("…", text: writable)` | `TextField.make(t -> t.placeholder(String).text(writable).secure(true))` | `TEXT_FIELD` 0x21 + `IS_SECURE` 0x200D |
| `TextEditor` | `TextEditor(text: writable)` | `TextEditor.make(t -> t.text(WritableSignal<String>))` | `TEXT_EDITOR` 0x22 |
| `Toggle` | `Toggle("label", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.make(t -> t.style(ToggleStyle).label(String).isOn(WritableSignal<Boolean>))` | `TOGGLE` 0x24; `VALUE_CHANGED` → value input; `TOGGLE_STYLE` 0x2018 |
| `Slider` | `Slider(value: writable, in: min...max)` | `Slider.make(s -> s.value(WritableSignal<Float>).min(float).max(float).onEditingChanged(Consumer<Boolean>))` | `SLIDER` 0x25; `VALUE_CHANGED` → value input |
| `Stepper` | `Stepper("label", value: writable, in: min...max, step:)` | `Stepper.make(s -> s.value(WritableSignal<Float>).min(float).max(float).step(float).label(String))` | `STEPPER` 0x26; `VALUE_CHANGED` → value input |
| `DatePicker` | `DatePicker("label", selection: writable, displayedComponents:)` | `DatePicker.make(d -> d.mode(DatePickerMode).selection(WritableSignal<Integer>))` | `DATE_PICKER` 0x27; `DATE_CHANGED` → date input; value via `PARAMETER::SET_DATE` |
| `Picker` | `Picker("label", selection: writable) { options }` | **content-bearing** — `Picker.make(p -> p.style(PickerStyle).selection(WritableSignal<Integer>)).children(View... options)` | `PICKER` 0x28; `VALUE_CHANGED` (index) → value input |

**Value bindings.** The value binding is a **config value** — the DSL reads the

# ADR-0014: Virtualized lazy stacks through app-owned data sources

**Status:** Accepted
**Recorded:** 2026-11-12
**Scope:** Authoring DSL, retained-tree emission, lazy-container layout, renderer realization, SSR first paint
**Supersedes:** None (refines the lazy-container realization wording in `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`)

## Context

Lazy stack and grid component IDs exist (`LAZY_VSTACK`, `LAZY_HSTACK`,
`LAZY_VGRID`, `LAZY_HGRID`), but the protocol only says a renderer MAY defer
realizing off-screen children. No item count, extent, visible-range request, or
window placement exists, so every implementation treats lazy containers as eager
aliases. Two constraints make the current wording insufficient:

- The app emits the full child list, and the desktop ring (4096 slots) and arena
  (1 MiB) cannot carry thousands of rows.
- A renderer cannot position or size an unrealized row without a size model, so
  it cannot compute scroll extent or decide what is visible.

The authoring surface must remain SwiftUI-shaped (ADR-0013):
`LazyVStack(spacing:) { ForEach(items) { … } }`, not a parallel
`VirtualVStack`.

## Decision

Virtualize lazy stacks through an app-owned data source and a renderer-reported
visible range.

- `ForEach` inside a `LAZY_VSTACK`/`LAZY_HSTACK` is a data source, not an eager
  child list. Outside a lazy container it keeps eager behavior.
- The app supplies the item collection and row builder; the engine owns the
  visible window and materializes only the window's rows.
- Fixed uniform extent: the engine derives `ITEM_EXTENT` from the row's fixed
  main-axis frame (`.frame(height:)` / `.frame(width:)`), or from an explicit
  `itemExtent` when no fixed frame exists.
- The wire carries `ITEM_COUNT`, `ITEM_EXTENT`, and `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` on the
  lazy container; the renderer reports `VISIBLE_RANGE` (first index + count) for
  nodes that declare listener bit 10.
- The lazy container occupies the full virtual main-axis extent
  (`N*E + max(0,N-1)*S`); emitted child `j` is placed at
  `(FIRST_ITEM_INDEX+j)*(E+S)`.
- Window children are reconciled by absolute index (or an optional item key), so
  ids stay stable while scrolling.
- SSR renders a conservative first window plus the full virtual extent; the
  client corrects the window after `META::ENVIRONMENT`.
- v1 covers `LAZY_VSTACK`/`LAZY_HSTACK`; lazy grids follow the same model in a
  later change.

Exact requirements live in `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`,
`spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, and `spec/DSL.md`.

## Rationale

- Only the window costs app nodes, wire bytes, renderer model memory, native
  elements, and SSR HTML; the full list can be arbitrarily large.
- The renderer stays stateless: it reports a measured/derived range, like
  `FIT_CHANGED`, and the app decides what to emit.
- The app-owned data source keeps the SwiftUI shape and avoids a second lazy
  authoring vocabulary.
- Fixed extent gives exact scroll extent and window math without measurement
  passes, matching the fixed-row-height pattern that avoids layout work.
- Windowed SSR avoids O(N) HTML while the full virtual extent keeps the
  scrollbar correct before JavaScript runs.

## Alternatives

- **Renderer-owned windowing with all children transmitted.** Rejected: O(N) app
  tree, wire, and renderer memory; overflows the desktop ring; cannot size
  unrealized rows; O(N) SSR.
- **Renderer pull by index.** Rejected for v1: adds a request/response handshake
  and renderer-owned item identity without removing the app's data-source work.
- **A separate `VirtualVStack`/`VirtualHStack` authoring API.** Rejected:
  confusing alongside `LazyVStack`, and contrary to the SwiftUI-shaped surface.
- **Variable-height first.** Deferred: needs estimation, measurement caching,
  and scroll anchoring; fixed extent covers the initial large-list use case.
- **Full SSR for every list.** Rejected as the default: O(N) HTML; remains
  available as an explicit host option for SEO-critical lists.

## Consequences

- New protocol properties (`ITEM_COUNT`, `ITEM_EXTENT`, `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX`),
  event (`VISIBLE_RANGE`), and listener bit (10) require Rust/Java/TS constants,
  manifest, codec, and conformance updates.
- The engine gains lazy-node window state and a keyed window reconcile;
  renderers gain virtual-extent placement and range reporting.
- Row-local component state is not preserved when a row leaves the window; apps
  should keep row state in the data model (keyed state is a follow-up).
- Lazy grids, variable-height rows, native recycling, scroll anchoring, and
  focused-row pinning remain follow-ups.
- The app must keep a focused row inside its window; the renderer does not
  auto-pin it.

## Sources and current contract

- Lazy container allocation: [PRIMITIVES.md §LazyVStack](../../spec/PRIMITIVES.md#lazyvstack--lazy_vstack-0x1b).
- Virtual extent and placement: [LAYOUT.md §Virtual extent](../../spec/LAYOUT.md#virtual-extent-lazy-containers).
- Event and listener: [EVENTS.md §Visible range](../../spec/EVENTS.md#visible-range), [§Event listeners](../../spec/EVENTS.md#event-listeners-event_listeners).
- Properties: [MODIFIERS.md §Layout](../../spec/MODIFIERS.md#1-layout).
- Authoring surface: [DSL.md §Virtualized lists](../../spec/DSL.md#virtualized-lists-lazyvstack--lazyhstack).
- Decisions: [ADR-0002](0002-native-declarative-layout.md),
  [ADR-0003](0003-application-state-and-delta-emission.md),
  [ADR-0011](0011-explicit-layout-allocation.md),
  [ADR-0013](0013-swiftui-shaped-signal-dsl.md).

Continued with the remaining implementation gaps.

**Rust DSL variable extents**
- Added `ForEach::item_extents(vec![…])` and `LazySource::extents()`.
- `build_lazy_stack` emits `ITEM_EXTENTS`, `FIRST_ITEM_OFFSET`, `TOTAL_EXTENT`, uses the average as `ITEM_EXTENT`, and sets each row’s main-axis size.
- Test: `lazy_vstack_for_each_uses_variable_extents`.

**Rust DSL lazy grids**
- `LazyVGrid`/`LazyHGrid` now consume a `ForEach` as a row/column unit window (`build_lazy_grid`), with `ITEM_COUNT` = units, `ITEM_EXTENT` = row/column extent, and only the visible units’ cells emitted.
- Tests: `lazy_vgrid_for_each_builds_a_row_window`, `lazy_hgrid_for_each_builds_a_column_window`.

**Qt lazy-grid padding**
- App padding now applies inside the virtual-extent wrapper (`plPad*`, offsetting the inner grid) instead of being ignored.
- Test: `lazy_grid_applies_app_padding_inside_the_wrapper`.
- Updated Qt status.

**Docs/status**
- Updated `spec/DSL.md`, `pathland-view/status.md`, `AGENTS.md`.

**Verified**
- Full `cargo test` passes (incl. 92 Qt tests); engine trace fixtures current; `git diff --check` clean.

**Remaining (architectural)**
- Keyed window reconcile for the Rust build-time engine (stable subtree ids).
- Focused-row pinning (needs a non-contiguous window representation / protocol addition + ADR).

Still uncommitted, including the earlier clamp fix.
commit and continue

This is **renderer state, not application state** (see
[ADR-0003](../docs/decisions/0003-application-state-and-delta-emission.md)): the
in-edit value is transient input/rendered-output state, like the scroll offset
and the text caret.

The session boundaries are also **reported as events** so the application can
suppress echoes of *derived* state the renderer cannot know about (a custom
drag offset, a drawn position):

- `FOCUS_CHANGED` (0x08) — the control gained/lost focus.
- `EDITING_CHANGED` (0x09) — a value/text edit session started/ended.

Both are reported **only when the target declared the matching `EVENT_LISTENERS`
bit** (`FOCUS` = `1<<5`, `EDITING` = `1<<6`). An application that observes
`EDITING_CHANGED { editing: true }` should hold back authoritative echoes of the
edited state until `{ editing: false }`.

The mechanism is **per-state / per-session**: implemented today for value drags
(`SLIDER`); text editing and other continuous inputs use the same path.

### Target resolution

The renderer resolves `targetId` from its own rendered-output tree (its
`id → native element` map): the event's position is hit-tested against that
--- focus detail ---
  component type.

### Text

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | SwiftUI counterpart |
| --------- | ------- | --- | --- | --- | ------- | --------------------- |
| `TEXT_CHANGED` | 0x07 | targetId | string offset | 0 | — | `TextField` value binding |
| `FOCUS_CHANGED` | 0x08 | targetId | focused (0/1) | 0 | — | `@FocusState` |
| `EDITING_CHANGED` | 0x09 | targetId | editing (0/1) | 0 | — | `TextField`/`Slider` `onEditingChanged` |
| `SUBMIT` | 0x0A | targetId | 0 | 0 | — | `TextField` `onSubmit` / `onCommit` |

- **`TEXT_CHANGED`**: the new text is a length-prefixed entry
  (`[u32 byteLength][bytes…]`). Over the **shared-memory ring** the renderer
  bump-allocates it into the host-owned **event arena** and `B` is its absolute
  offset (see OPCODE.md); over the **network** it lives in the batch's string
  section referenced by a *relative* `B` offset — exactly the `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT`
  dual convention. A bare opcode cannot resolve the text; batch-aware decoders
  (`pathland-core-transport`, Java `FrameCodec`, TS `decoder.ts`) resolve it.
  The event is reported on **every** edit, including intermediate edits, not
  only on commit.
- **`FOCUS_CHANGED`**: `B` = 1 gained focus, 0 lost focus. The renderer reports
  it for nodes that declared the `FOCUS` listener bit (bit 5). Focus is what
  routes subsequent `KEY_*` events.
- **`EDITING_CHANGED`**: `B` = 1 editing session began, 0 ended. Reported for
  nodes that declared the `EDITING` listener bit (bit 6).
- **`SUBMIT`**: the user committed the field (Enter). Reported for nodes that
  declared the `SUBMIT` listener bit (bit 7). `B` MAY carry the current text as
  a string-section offset (reserved for future use; 0 today).

## Event listeners (`EVENT_LISTENERS`)

`EVENT_LISTENERS` (0x2005) is a u32 bitmask set via `SET_PROPERTY` (U32). Each
bit requests one raw-input event kind for the node:

| Bit | Mask | Event |
| ----- | ------ | ------- |
| 0 | `0x00000001` | `POINTER_DOWN` |
| 1 | `0x00000002` | `POINTER_MOVE` (incl. hover enter/leave) |
| 2 | `0x00000004` | `POINTER_UP` |
| 3 | `0x00000008` | `KEY_DOWN` |
| 4 | `0x00000010` | `KEY_UP` |
| 5 | `0x00000020` | `FOCUS_CHANGED` |
| 6 | `0x00000040` | `EDITING_CHANGED` |
| 7 | `0x00000080` | `SUBMIT` |
| 8 | `0x00000100` | `SCROLL` |
| 9 | `0x00000200` | `WHEEL` |
| 10 | `0x00000400` | `VISIBLE_RANGE` |
| 11–31 | — | reserved |

Convenience aliases (DSL-side): `POINTER = bits 0|1|2`.

# Focused-row pinning — walkthrough

## What the feature means
When a control inside a lazy row has keyboard focus, the row must stay mounted even if the user scrolls it out of the visible window. If the row is evicted, its native element is deleted, focus is lost, and a re-entered row gets a fresh widget. “Pinning” keeps the focused row alive; when focus is lost, it unpins.

## Why it does not work today

There are two independent gaps.

### 1. The app cannot observe focus

Renderers already emit `FOCUS_CHANGED` for nodes that declare `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit 5:

- GTK: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:778`
- Qt: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-qt/src/qt/qt_layer.cpp:3286` (currently only text inputs)
- DOM: `lib/typescript/src/index.ts:390`

But the JVM side drops it:

- `InputDispatcher.dispatch` routes text/value/editing/date/media/fit/visible-range — no focus branch (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/engine/InputDispatcher.kt:38`).
- `RenderResult` has no focus map (`RenderResult.kt:8`).
- `PathlandNode` has no focus callback (`PathlandNode.kt:60-68`).
- The DSL has no `.onFocusChanged`; only `pointerEvents(mask)` sets the listener bit (`spec/DSL.md:1002`, `Modifiers.kt:404`).

So even if the engine knew which row to pin, the app has no way to tell it which row is focused.

### 2. The lazy window is contiguous

The wire model is a single contiguous window:

- `ITEM_COUNT`, `ITEM_EXTENT`, `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (`spec/LAYOUT.md:192`).
- Emitted child `j` is placed at `(FIRST_ITEM_INDEX + j) * (E + S)`; the window need not cover every unit.
- `LazyStackView` derives the window only from `VISIBLE_RANGE` (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt:170`).
- HTML uses flex + virtual padding, GTK/Qt use leading/trailing spacers, DOM uses padding — all assume contiguous children.

If the focused row is outside the window, there is no representation for “visible window **plus** one row at index 47”. The engine deletes the row, the renderer deletes the widget, and focus dies.

Keyed reconcile (commit `0505b268`) helps only when the row **remains** in the window: retained rows keep their ids. It does not keep an evicted row mounted.

## Options

### Option A — Focus binding + window union (no protocol change)

The lazy stack takes a pinned index (or key). The engine sets:

```
window = (visibleStart - overscan) .. (visibleEnd + overscan)
union with pinnedIndex
```

Pros:
- Spec-compliant: the app owns overscan and may emit a larger window; `LAYOUT.md` already allows windows that do not cover every unit.
- No new opcode/property, no manifest/codec/renderer changes.
- Delivers the fix quickly and works on all renderers that already report focus.

Cons:
- The window is contiguous, so pinning a far-away row emits every row in between — `O(gap)`.
- The app should clear the pin when the focused row is far outside the viewport (or accept the cost).
- Qt currently reports focus only for text inputs; a focusable `Button` row would not report it without widening the Qt focus hook.

### Option B — Pinned child + protocol property

Keep the visible window virtualized and emit the pinned row as an **extra child** at its absolute offset. Add a property such as `PINNED_ITEM_INDEX` (`0x0028`, U32) and a convention (e.g. the last child is the pinned row). Renderers place it absolutely / with an extra spacer.

Pros:
- No `O(gap)`; true virtualization.
- Pinned row survives even when the viewport is far away.

Cons:
- Requires an ADR (protocol change), `spec/LAYOUT.md`, `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, constants, manifest, Java/TS mirrors, conformance vectors.
- HTML/DOM need absolute positioning for the pinned child; GTK/Qt need a third spacer/section; all renderers need tests.
- More moving parts and a larger review surface.

### Rejected
- Renderer keeps the focused widget alive after the app deletes the row: violates renderer statelessness.
- Blur on eviction: a fallback, not pinning.

## Recommended plan

I recommend **Option A first**, then Option B only if the `O(gap)` cost proves unacceptable.

### Phase 1 — Focus observation (needed either way)

JVM/web:
1. `PathlandNode`: add `focusInput: Consumer<Boolean>?`.
2. `Emitter`: add `focusInputs`, collect `node.focusInput` like `editingInput`, remove on delete, clear on mount, expose in `RenderResult`.
3. `RenderResult`: add `focusInputs()`.
4. `InputDispatcher`: `event.isFocusChanged -> focusInputs[event.target()]?.accept(event.b() != 0)`.
5. DSL: add `View.onFocusChanged { focused -> … }` (or `focusable(WritableSignal<Boolean>)`). It sets `Commands.Listeners.FOCUS` and `node.focusInput`.
6. Tests: mount a view with `.onFocusChanged`, dispatch `Event.focusChanged(target, true/false)`, assert the callback/signal; assert the listener bit is emitted.
7. Spec: update `spec/DSL.md` §5.5 (replace “no per-event sugar” for focus) and `spec/MODIFIERS.md` §semantic.
8. Qt: widen `activeFocusChanged` to any node with the FOCUS listener bit, not just text inputs. GTK/DOM already do.

Rust parity (optional in Phase 1): add `InputHandlers.focus` and route `Event::FocusChanged`; the GTK/Qt demos can then observe focus.

### Phase 2A — Window union

1. `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack`/`ForEach`: add `pinned: Signal<Int?>?` (or `pinnedKey`).
2. `LazyStackView`: read the pinned signal; union it into `initialWindow` and the `visibleRangeInput` window.
3. App wiring: the row’s `.onFocusChanged` sets a `focusedIndex`/`focusedKey` signal; the lazy stack receives it.
4. Test: pin a far index, assert the window includes it and the row is emitted; clear, assert the window returns to the visible range.
5. Document the `O(gap)` behavior and recommend clearing the pin beyond a threshold.

### Phase 2B — Protocol pinned child (if chosen)

1. ADR proposal (Proposed, not accepted): pinned-row placement.
2. `PINNED_ITEM_INDEX` (`0x0028`) in spec + constants + manifest + Java/TS mirrors.
3. Engine emits the pinned child last; `ITEM_EXTENTS`/`FIRST_ITEM_OFFSET`/`TOTAL_EXTENT` remain the window’s.
4. Renderers: HTML/DOM absolute placement; GTK/Qt extra spacer/section.
5. Conformance vectors + renderer tests.

### Phase 3 — Rust DSL parity

Mirror Phase 1/2 in `pathland-view`/`pathland-engine`: `Node.focus_input`, `InputHandlers.focus`, `ForEach::pinned`, and `build_lazy_stack` window union.

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Model:** Option A (window union, no protocol change) or Option B (protocol pinned child)?
2. **Scope:** JVM/web first, or all renderers and the Rust DSL in the same change?
3. **Far-away focus:** expand the window and keep focus, or let the app clear the pin/blur when the row is more than N units outside the viewport?

My recommendation: Option A, JVM/web first, with an app-side distance threshold; revisit Option B via an ADR if the gap cost matters.
Could we add this as a follow up issue?

**Title**
`feat(lazy): focused-row pinning for lazy stacks`

**Labels**
`enhancement`

**Body**

> **Context**
> ADR-0014 follow-up. Lazy stacks virtualize rows, but a focused control inside a row loses focus when the row scrolls out of the window and is evicted. The row (and its native element) is deleted, then recreated on re-entry.
>
> **Problem**
> Two gaps:
>
> 1. **Focus is not observable by the app.** Renderers emit `FOCUS_CHANGED` for nodes with `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit 5 (GTK `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:778`, DOM `lib/typescript/src/index.ts:390`; Qt currently only for text inputs, `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-qt/src/qt/qt_layer.cpp:3286`). The JVM host drops the event: `InputDispatcher` has no focus branch (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/engine/InputDispatcher.kt:38`), `RenderResult` has no focus map, `PathlandNode` has no focus callback, and the DSL has no `.onFocusChanged` (only `pointerEvents(mask)`).
> 2. **The lazy window is contiguous.** `ITEM_COUNT`/`ITEM_EXTENT`/`FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` place emitted child `j` at `(FIRST_ITEM_INDEX+j)*(E+S)` (`spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent). A row outside the window cannot be “kept mounted” without either expanding the contiguous range or adding a non-contiguous pinned child.
>
> Keyed window reconcile (commit `0505b268`) keeps ids for rows that **remain** in the window; it does not keep an evicted row mounted.
>
> **Proposed scope**
>
> **Phase 1 — focus observation (needed either way)**
> - `PathlandNode.focusInput`, `Emitter.focusInputs`, `RenderResult.focusInputs`.
> - `InputDispatcher`: route `FOCUS_CHANGED` to the target’s callback.
> - DSL `.onFocusChanged { focused -> … }` (sets `Commands.Listeners.FOCUS`).
> - Qt: report focus for any node with the FOCUS listener bit, not only text inputs.
> - Tests + spec/status updates.
>
> **Phase 2A — window union (recommended v1)**
> - `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack` take a pinned index/key signal.
> - The engine unions the pinned index into the visible window.
> - No protocol change; spec-compliant overscan. Cost: `O(gap)` when the pinned row is far away; the app should clear the pin beyond a threshold.
>
> **Phase 2B — protocol pinned child (alternative, needs ADR)**
> - Add `PINNED_ITEM_INDEX` (`0x0028`, U32); emit the pinned row as an extra child at its absolute offset.
> - Renderer placement: HTML/DOM absolute; GTK/Qt extra spacer/section.
> - Full protocol/manifest/Java/TS/conformance updates.
>
> **Phase 3 — Rust DSL parity**
> - `Node.focus_input`, `InputHandlers.focus`, `ForEach::pinned`, window union in `build_lazy_stack`.
>
> **Acceptance criteria**
> - A focusable row reports focus to the app on JVM/web (and GTK/Qt).
> - A focused row remains mounted when scrolled out of the visible window.
> - Focus survives an overlapping window slide; unpin on focus loss.
> - No regressions in lazy-stack/grid rendering or deltas.
> - If 2B is chosen: protocol, manifest, Java/TS mirrors, conformance vectors, and renderer tests.
>
> **Decision points**
> - Phase 2A (window union) vs 2B (protocol pinned child).
> - JVM/web first vs all renderers/Rust DSL in one change.
> - Far-away focus: expand the window vs clear the pin/blur.
>
> **References**
> - ADR-0014, `spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent, `spec/EVENTS.md` §Text/`FOCUS_CHANGED`, `spec/DSL.md` §5.5/§Virtualized lists.
> - `lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt`, `.../engine/InputDispatcher.kt`, `.../engine/RenderResult.kt`, `.../engine/PathlandNode.kt`.

## Context

ADR-0014 follow-up. Lazy stacks virtualize rows, but a focused control inside a row loses focus when the row scrolls out of the window and is evicted. The row (and its native element) is deleted, then recreated on re-entry.

**Chosen model:** Option A — focus observation plus a contiguous window union (no protocol change). Rust DSL parity is included in this issue.

## Problem

Two gaps:

1. **Focus is not observable by the app.** Renderers emit `FOCUS_CHANGED` for nodes with `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit 5 (GTK `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:778`, DOM `lib/typescript/src/index.ts:390`; Qt currently only for text inputs, `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-qt/src/qt/qt_layer.cpp:3286`). The JVM host drops the event: `InputDispatcher` has no focus branch (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/engine/InputDispatcher.kt:38`), `RenderResult` has no focus map, `PathlandNode` has no focus callback, and the DSL has no `.onFocusChanged` (only `pointerEvents(mask)`).
2. **The lazy window is contiguous.** `ITEM_COUNT`/`ITEM_EXTENT`/`FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` place emitted child `j` at `(FIRST_ITEM_INDEX+j)*(E+S)` (`spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent). A row outside the window cannot be "kept mounted" without expanding the contiguous range.

Keyed window reconcile (commit `0505b268`) keeps ids for rows that **remain** in the window; it does not keep an evicted row mounted.

## Proposed scope (Option A)

### Phase 1 — focus observation

JVM/web:
- `PathlandNode.focusInput` (`Consumer<Boolean>?`).
- `Emitter.focusInputs` (collect/clear like `editingInput`), exposed via `RenderResult.focusInputs`.
- `InputDispatcher`: route `FOCUS_CHANGED` to `focusInputs[target]?.accept(b != 0)`.
- DSL: `View.onFocusChanged { focused -> … }` (sets `Commands.Listeners.FOCUS` and `node.focusInput`).
- Tests: mount with `.onFocusChanged`, dispatch `Event.focusChanged(target, true/false)`, assert the callback/signal and the emitted listener bit.
- Spec: update `spec/DSL.md` §5.5 and `spec/MODIFIERS.md` §semantic.

Qt:
- Report focus for any node with the FOCUS listener bit, not only text inputs. GTK/DOM already do.

### Phase 2 — pinned-row window union

- `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack` (and the underlying `ForEach`) take a pinned index/key signal.
- `LazyStackView` reads the pin and unions it into `initialWindow` and the `VISIBLE_RANGE` window:
  `window = (visibleStart - overscan) .. (visibleEnd + overscan)` ∪ `pinnedIndex`.
- App wiring: a row's `.onFocusChanged` sets a `focusedIndex`/`focusedKey` signal; the lazy stack receives it.
- The pin is cleared on focus loss.
- Document the `O(gap)` behavior: the app should clear the pin when the row is more than N units outside the viewport.
- Test: pin a far index, assert the window includes it and the row is emitted; clear, assert the window returns to the visible range.

### Phase 3 — Rust DSL parity

- `Node.focus_input` + `InputHandlers.focus`; route `Event::FocusChanged` in the Rust demos.
- `ForEach::pinned` (or an equivalent pinned-index handle).
- `build_lazy_stack` unions the pinned index into the window.
- Tests mirroring the JVM/web pin/window behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- A focusable row reports focus to the app on JVM/web (and GTK/Qt).
- A focused row remains mounted when scrolled out of the visible window.
- Focus survives an overlapping window slide; unpin on focus loss.
- The window union is covered by JVM and Rust DSL tests; no regressions in lazy-stack/grid rendering or deltas.
- Spec/status/ADR-0014 follow-up notes updated.

## References

- ADR-0014, `spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent, `spec/EVENTS.md` §Text/`FOCUS_CHANGED`, `spec/DSL.md` §5.5/§Virtualized lists.
- `lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt`, `.../engine/InputDispatcher.kt`, `.../engine/RenderResult.kt`, `.../engine/PathlandNode.kt`.
- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-view/src/lib.rs`, `lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine/src/node.rs`.
- Keyed reconcile: commit `0505b268`.

## Why the blank appears

The list already pre-renders, but only **2 rows** past each edge:

- `OVERSCAN = 2` (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt:18`)
- On a `VISIBLE_RANGE` report the window becomes `visibleStart - 2 .. visibleEnd + 2` (`LazyList.kt:171`).
- The DOM client computes the visible range and sends it over the WebSocket (`lib/typescript/src/apply.ts:2571`, `refreshLazyWindows`).
- The server’s batcher adds up to **20 ms** (`DeltaBatcher.java:36`), then the network round trip, then the delta is applied.

So at 64 pt rows the prefetch buffer is ~128 px. A fast wheel/flick can move several hundred pixels before the round trip completes; the virtual padding reserves the space, but the rows have not arrived yet, so you see the blank area.

## The fix

Make overscan an explicit, app-owned lazy-stack parameter and give the demo a larger buffer.

### 1. Kotlin DSL

Add `overscan: Int = 2` to:

- `LazyVStack` / `LazyHStack` (all spacing overloads)
- `LazyVGrid` / `LazyHGrid`
- internal `LazyStackView` / `LazyGridWindowView`

Replace the private `OVERSCAN` constant with the constructor value in:

- `initialWindow` (`LazyList.kt:222`, `:361`)
- the `VISIBLE_RANGE` window calculation (`:171`, `:309`)

Keep the **default at 2** so existing tests and the `lazy_window_mount` engine trace (which expects 22 rows) stay unchanged.

### 2. Demo

In `LibraryView` set a larger buffer, e.g.:

```kotlin
LazyVStack(spacing = 0f, overscan = 12) { … }
```

12 rows × 64 pt = 768 px, which covers the batcher + round trip for normal scrolling. Tune to 8–16 depending on how aggressive the scroll is.

### 3. Tests

- Add a `DslTest` case: `LazyVStack(overscan = 5)` → initial window has `DEFAULT_WINDOW + 5` rows; `onVisibleRange(50, 5)` emits `visible + 2*5` rows.
- Existing default-overscan tests remain valid.
- Add a demo-view test or status note for the larger buffer.

### 4. Spec / status

- `spec/DSL.md` §Virtualized lists: document `overscan` (rows, default 2) as the app-owned prefetch buffer; the engine emits `visible ± overscan`.
- `spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent already says the app owns overscan; link the new parameter.
- Update `pathland-view-core/status.md` and the demo status.

### 5. Rust DSL parity

The Rust `ForEach` window is host-managed (`window_handle()`), so add a small helper rather than engine magic:

- `ForEach::overscan(n)` storing the buffer.
- `ForEach::set_visible_range(first, count)` that sets the window to `first - n .. first + count + n`, clamped.
- Update the Rust demo/host to call it on `VISIBLE_RANGE`.

This keeps the Rust host in control while matching the JVM default.

## Alternatives considered

- **Velocity-aware prefetch**: the DOM client could add a forward margin proportional to scroll velocity. More accurate, but more complex and stateful; a larger fixed overscan is simpler and covers the latency.
- **Lower the server flush interval** for lazy deltas: helps a little, but does not solve a fast flick.
- **Placeholder/skeleton rows**: avoids blank but shows fake content; the user asked for real pre-rendered entries.

Yes. Instead of an author-facing `overscan` value, make the prefetch an **engine-derived reactive margin**: the engine already receives a stream of `VISIBLE_RANGE` reports and already owns a `WritableSignal<IntRange>` window. It can derive the margin from the observed scroll velocity on each report.

## Reactive prefetch model

Per lazy stack/grid view, keep the previous report:

```kotlin
private var lastVisible: IntRange? = null
private var lastVisibleAt: Long = 0L
```

On each `VISIBLE_RANGE(first, count)`:

```kotlin
val now = System.nanoTime()
val previous = lastVisible
val delta = if (previous == null) 0 else first - previous.first
val elapsedMs = if (previous == null) 0.0 else (now - lastVisibleAt) / 1_000_000.0
lastVisible = first until (first + count)
lastVisibleAt = now

val velocity = if (elapsedMs > 0.0) abs(delta) / elapsedMs else 0.0
val extra = if (delta == 0) 0
            else ceil(velocity * LATENCY_BUDGET_MS).toInt()
                .coerceIn(0, MAX_PREFETCH - BASE_OVERSCAN)

val start = (first - BASE_OVERSCAN - if (delta < 0) extra else 0).coerceAtLeast(0)
val end = (first + count - 1 + BASE_OVERSCAN + if (delta > 0) extra else 0)
    .coerceAtMost(total - 1)
windowSignal.set(if (end >= start) start..end else IntRange.EMPTY)
```

- **Directional:** extra rows are prefetched only in the direction of travel; the opposite side keeps the small base.
- **First report:** no previous report → base only. Existing tests that call `onVisibleRange` once keep their current expectations.
- **Decay:** the next report with `delta == 0` returns to base. If no further report arrives, the window stays at the last prefetch, bounded by the cap.
- **No new protocol, no app configuration.** The window is still a signal, so the emitter diffs and only the entering/leaving rows emit.

## Internal constants (not author-configurable)

| Constant | Suggested value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `BASE_OVERSCAN` | `2` | Current behavior; small buffer for jitter and the first report |
| `LATENCY_BUDGET_MS` | `120` | Covers the 20 ms batcher + network + render |
| `MAX_PREFETCH` | `max(2 * visibleCount, 24)` | Bounds cost on huge jumps (scrollbar drags) |

These live next to the existing `OVERSCAN`/`DEFAULT_WINDOW` in `LazyList.kt`.

## Where it goes

- `LazyStackView` (`lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt`) — replace the `OVERSCAN` constant in `initialWindow`/`visibleRangeInput` with the derived margin.
- `LazyGridWindowView` — same logic in unit space.
- `initialWindow` keeps the base margin; it has no velocity sample yet.

## Tests

- New `DslTest`: mount a lazy stack, report `onVisibleRange(0, 5)` (seeds the previous range), then `onVisibleRange(50, 5)` (large delta → capped prefetch). Assert `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` and that the emitted window extends beyond `visible + base` by the cap.
- Existing single-report tests remain valid (first report → base).
- Add a small-delta case (e.g. 1 row) asserting the base window.
- The `lazy_window_mount` engine trace uses the initial window and is unaffected.

## Spec / decision

`spec/LAYOUT.md:234` currently says:

> The application owns overscan and may emit a larger window.

That changes to an engine-owned policy, e.g.:

> The engine may prefetch a bounded margin in the scroll direction, derived from the visible-range report velocity; the margin is engine-owned and not author-configured. The application may still emit a larger window.

This is a contract change. Do you want:

- a direct `spec/LAYOUT.md` + `spec/DSL.md` update, or
- a short Proposed ADR for the engine-owned adaptive prefetch?

## Rust parity

The Rust `ForEach` window is host-managed (`window_handle()`), so the adaptive logic belongs in the host/demo, not the `no_std` `pathland-view` crate. The host can mirror the same formula with `std::time::Instant` and call `window.set(...)` on `VISIBLE_RANGE`. I can include a small host-side helper in the same change if you want desktop parity.

## Questions

1. Velocity model: **time-based** (rows/ms × latency budget, recommended) or a simpler **delta × multiplier**?
2. Are the internal constants (`2`, `120 ms`, `2× viewport / 24`) acceptable?
3. Should the DOM client force a final report on `scrollend` so the prefetch decays immediately, or accept the capped window until the next scroll?
4. Direct spec update or Proposed ADR for the engine-owned prefetch?
5. Include the Rust host-side helper in this change?

ADRs explain **why** Pathland makes consequential architectural choices.
[`spec/`](../../spec/) defines the **current contract**; each implementing

## Conventions

Source-reference syntax, review obligations, drift resolution, and validation
commands are defined in [Architecture traceability and drift](traceability.md).
The [Pathland architecture skills](skills.md) provide reusable orientation,
decision-authoring, review, and maintenance workflows for these conventions.

- Use `NNNN-short-decision-name.md`, allocated sequentially. Never reuse a
  published number. Resolve provisional number collisions before merging.
- Start with [the template](template.md). Keep context, decision, rationale,
  alternatives, consequences, and source links distinct.
- Status is **Proposed**, **Accepted**, **Rejected**, or **Superseded**. A

# Implementation plan — reactive lazy prefetch

## Decision

Replace the fixed, author-configurable overscan with an **engine-derived, directional prefetch** computed from the `VISIBLE_RANGE` report velocity. No new protocol property and no app-facing configuration.

Internal constants:

- `BASE_OVERSCAN = 2` rows (jitter / first report)
- `LATENCY_BUDGET_MS = 120.0` (batcher + network + render)
- `MAX_PREFETCH = max(2 * visibleCount, 24)` units

The window remains a `WritableSignal<IntRange>`, so only entering/leaving rows emit.

## 1. ADR + spec

- Add `docs/decisions/0015-reactive-lazy-prefetch.md` from `docs/decisions/template.md`.
  - Status: **Proposed** until you accept it.
  - Decision: engine-owned, bounded, directional prefetch derived from visible-range velocity; app may still emit a larger window.
  - Rationale: removes blank rows during fast scroll without author tuning; uses the existing event stream; bounded cost.
  - Alternatives: app-configured overscan (rejected), renderer-reported prefetch margin (conflates visible semantics), placeholders, keeping evicted rows (violates renderer statelessness).
  - Consequences: `spec/LAYOUT.md` / `spec/DSL.md` / `spec/EVENTS.md` updates; DOM final report; Rust host helper.
- Update `docs/decisions/README.md` index with ADR-0015 (Proposed).
- Update `spec/LAYOUT.md:234`:
  - Replace “The application owns overscan and may emit a larger window.” with: the engine may prefetch a bounded margin in the scroll direction derived from report velocity; engine-owned, not author-configured; the application may still emit a larger window.
- Update `spec/DSL.md` §Virtualized lists with a short prefetch bullet.
- Update `spec/EVENTS.md` §Visible range: a renderer SHOULD report the final range when a scroll gesture ends so the engine can release prefetched rows.

## 2. JVM engine

In `lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/dsl/LazyList.kt`:

- Add internal fields to `LazyStackView` and `LazyGridWindowView`:
  ```kotlin
  private var lastVisible: IntRange? = null
  private var lastVisibleAt = 0L
  ```
- Keep `initialWindow` on `BASE_OVERSCAN`.
- Replace the `OVERSCAN` use in `visibleRangeInput` (`:171`, `:309`) with:
  ```kotlin
  val now = System.nanoTime()
  val previous = lastVisible
  val delta = if (previous == null) 0 else firstVisible - previous.first
  val elapsedMs = if (previous == null) 0.0
                  else ((now - lastVisibleAt) / 1_000_000.0).coerceAtLeast(0.1)
  lastVisible = firstVisible until (firstVisible + visibleCount)
  lastVisibleAt = now

  val velocity = if (previous == null || delta == 0) 0.0
                 else abs(delta) / elapsedMs
  val maxExtra = (maxOf(2 * visibleCount, 24) - BASE_OVERSCAN).coerceAtLeast(0)
  val extra = ceil(velocity * LATENCY_BUDGET_MS).toInt().coerceIn(0, maxExtra)

  val start = (firstVisible - BASE_OVERSCAN - if (delta < 0) extra else 0)
      .coerceAtLeast(0)
  val end = (firstVisible + visibleCount - 1 + BASE_OVERSCAN +
      if (delta > 0) extra else 0).coerceAtMost(total - 1)
  windowSignal.set(if (end >= start) start..end else IntRange.EMPTY)
  ```
- Apply the same logic to the grid in unit space.
- First report → `delta == 0` → base, so existing single-report tests and the `lazy_window_mount` trace are unchanged.
- A repeated report with the same range (`delta == 0`) decays to base.

## 3. DOM client final report

In `lib/typescript/src/apply.ts`:

- Add a `force` parameter to `refreshLazyWindows(r, force = false)` that bypasses the `lazyRanges` cache when true.
- In `lib/typescript/src/index.ts`:
  - On `scrollend` (capture), call `refreshLazyWindows(renderer, true)`.
  - Add a 150 ms debounce fallback after the last scroll for browsers without `scrollend`; clear it on each scroll.
- The final report sends the same range; the engine sees `delta == 0` and shrinks the window to base.
- Add a DOM test that a forced refresh emits `VISIBLE_RANGE` even when the range is unchanged.

## 4. Rust parity

In `lib/rust/crates/pathland-view/src/lib.rs`:

- Add a `VisibleWindow` handle:
  ```rust

      window: Rc<Cell<(usize, usize)>>,
      last: Cell<Option<(usize, usize)>>,
      total: usize,
  }
  impl VisibleWindow {
      pub fn set_visible_range(&self, first: usize, count: usize, elapsed_ms: f32) { … }

Rust:

- `lib/typescript/status.md`: forced final report on scroll end/debounce.
- `lib/rust/crates/pathland-view/status.md`: `VisibleWindow` helper.
- `lib/java/pathland-demo-views-kotlin/status.md`: note the library blank is fixed without app changes (no `overscan` config).
- `AGENTS.md`: add “engine-derived reactive lazy prefetch” to the lazy-stack status.
- `spec/LAYOUT.md`, `spec/DSL.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, ADR index.

- `cd lib/java && mvn -q -P jvm-only test`
- `cd lib/rust && cargo test -q`
- `cargo run -q -p pathland-engine-golden -- --check` (initial window unchanged)
- `npm --prefix lib/typescript run typecheck && npm --prefix lib/typescript test`

## Notes / risks

- The cap bounds cost on huge scrollbar jumps; a jump larger than the cap may still briefly blank, but wheel/flick scrolling is covered.
- The first report always uses base; the prefetch starts on the second report.
- `elapsedMs` is floored at 0.1 ms to avoid division by zero; tests use an explicit sleep.
- ADR-0015 stays **Proposed** until you accept it; the spec update lands with the implementation as the current contract.

# ADR-0015: Engine-derived reactive prefetch for lazy windows

**Status:** Proposed
**Recorded:** 2026-11-16
**Scope:** Authoring DSL, engine lazy-window policy, renderer visible-range reporting
**Supersedes:** None (refines the lazy-window policy described in `spec/LAYOUT.md`)

## Context

A windowed lazy stack/grid renders only the rows the application emitted. The
renderer reports `VISIBLE_RANGE` after scrolling, the engine re-renders the
window, and the delta travels back to the renderer. With a fixed two-row
overscan, a fast scroll can move farther than the prefetch buffer before the
round trip completes, leaving a blank region where rows have not arrived yet.

Making overscan an author-facing setting would push a renderer-latency concern
into application code. The engine already receives a stream of visible-range
reports and already owns the window signal, so it can derive the prefetch
itself.

## Decision

The engine derives a bounded, directional prefetch margin from the observed
visible-range velocity. No author-facing overscan setting and no new protocol
property.

- The renderer continues to report the visible range (`VISIBLE_RANGE`).
- The engine keeps the previous report `(first, count)` and its arrival time.
- On each report it computes `velocity = |delta| / elapsed`, then
  `extra = ceil(velocity * latencyBudget)`, clamped to a bounded maximum.
- Extra rows are prefetched in the direction of travel; a small base margin is
  kept on both sides.
- A report with no movement returns the window to the base margin.
- Renderers SHOULD report a final range when a scroll gesture ends so the
  prefetch decays promptly.
- The application may still emit a larger window when it has its own reasons.

Exact requirements live in `spec/LAYOUT.md` §Virtual extent, `spec/DSL.md`
§Virtualized lists, and `spec/EVENTS.md` §Visible range.

## Rationale

- The blank region is a renderer/transport latency problem, not an application
  layout choice; the engine is the component that owns the window and sees the
  report cadence.
- The velocity signal is already implicit in successive visible ranges, so the
  change adds no protocol surface and works for every renderer.
- The base margin preserves the existing behavior for the first report and for
  slow scrolling.
- The bounded maximum prevents a large scrollbar jump from emitting an
  unbounded number of rows.

## Alternatives

- **Author-configured overscan.** Rejected by the maintainer: it moves a
  renderer-latency tuning knob into application code and would need a DSL
  surface for every lazy container.
- **Renderer-reported prefetch margin.** Rejected: it would conflate “visible”
  with “prefetched” in `VISIBLE_RANGE`, and renderers do not own the window
  policy.
- **Placeholder/skeleton rows.** Rejected: avoids blank space but shows fake
  content; the goal is to render real rows ahead of the viewport.
- **Keep evicted rows mounted until replacements arrive.** Rejected: the
  application owns the retained tree; retaining deleted rows violates renderer
  statelessness and can show stale content.

## Consequences

- `spec/LAYOUT.md` changes overscan ownership from the application to an
  engine-owned adaptive margin (the application may still emit a larger window).
- The JVM engine and the Rust host helper implement the same formula; the
  renderer event surface is unchanged.
- Renderers should send a final range on scroll end (DOM: `scrollend` plus a
  debounce fallback).
- The prefetch is bounded; a scrollbar jump larger than the bound may still
  briefly blank, but wheel/flick scrolling is covered.
- The first report always uses the base margin; adaptive prefetch starts on the
  second report.

## Sources and current contract

- Lazy window placement: [LAYOUT.md §Virtual extent](../../spec/LAYOUT.md#virtual-extent-lazy-containers).
- Authoring rules: [DSL.md §Virtualized lists](../../spec/DSL.md#virtualized-lists-lazyvstack--lazyhstack).
- Visible-range event: [EVENTS.md §Visible range](../../spec/EVENTS.md#visible-range).
- Related decisions: [ADR-0014](0014-virtualized-lazy-stacks.md).

content.text:
Short answer: **not directly today.** `ForEach` accepts only a `List<T>` or a `Signal<List<T>>`:

```kotlin
fun <T> ForEach(items: List<T>, ...)
fun <T> ForEach(items: Signal<List<T>>, ...)
```

The lazy window needs three things a stream generally does not provide:

- a stable **size** (`ITEM_COUNT`, `data.count()`),
- **random access by absolute index** (`data.row(index)` → `list[index]`),
- **re-evaluation on every render/window slide** (`ForEachView` reads the list again each time).

So a one-shot `java.util.stream.Stream` or `Sequence` cannot be used directly, and an infinite stream has no finite `ITEM_COUNT` at all.

## What works

**Finite stream** — materialize once:

```kotlin
ForEach(stream.toList()) { item, _ -> … }
```

**Reactive/async stream** — collect into a signal on the session actor, then pass the signal:

```kotlin
val tracks = mutableState<List<Track>>(emptyList())
// session-scoped collection (or marshal via PathlandSession.submit/topic)
scope.launch { flow.collect { tracks.set(it) } }

LazyVStack { ForEach(tracks) { track, _ -> TrackRow(track) } }
```

**Rust** — `ForEach::new(iterator.collect::<Vec<_>>(), …)`.

## What does not work

- `Stream<T>` / `Sequence<T>` directly (one-shot, no `size`/`get`).
- `Flow<T>` / `Flux` / Rx directly (the view layer does not own a collection scope or lifecycle).
- Infinite/paged streams (no finite `ITEM_COUNT`; no random access).

## If you want first-class stream support

Three possible directions:

1. **Materializing overloads** — `ForEach(sequence: Sequence<T>)` / `ForEach(stream: Stream<T>)` that consume the stream once into a list at construction. Simple, but not reactive and one-shot streams cannot be re-read on a later render.
2. **Flow adapter** — a helper that collects a `Flow<List<T>>` into a `Signal<List<T>>` with an explicit session/coroutine scope. The DSL shouldn’t own the scope; this belongs in the app/server layer.
3. **Paged data source** — a `LazyDataSource` abstraction with `count` plus `get(index)`/page loading and a signal that updates as pages arrive. This is a larger design: the protocol’s `ITEM_COUNT` must grow/estimate, and rows that are not loaded yet need a placeholder or a fetch contract. That would be ADR-worthy.

Which kind of “stream” do you mean — Java/Kotlin `Stream`/`Sequence`, coroutine `Flow`/Reactor/Rx, or a paged database cursor? That determines whether this is a small overload or a new data-source abstraction.
What I need is an easy way to use data from different datasources like databases or rest apis.

result.output:
# External UI updates with topic subscriptions

Pathland signals are single-threaded by contract: reads, writes, and effects run
on the session's actor. Background work (Kafka/SmallRye `@Incoming` consumers,
scheduled jobs, database notifications, other transports) runs on its own
threads, so it must not set a view's signal directly.

Topic subscriptions are the supported bridge. A view subscribes to a
**strongly typed, always-scoped** topic and gets a normal `Signal<T>`; external
code publishes a value for the same `(topic, subject)` pair from any thread, and
only the sessions subscribed to that pair update. The runtime applies the value
on each session's actor, so the existing effect/delta path is unchanged.

## 1. Declare the topic once

A `Topic<T, S>` carries the payload type `T` and the subject type `S`. Topic
identity is its name, so the view and the publisher share the same constant.

```kotlin
object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic.of("customer.name")
    val ORDERS: Topic<List<Order>, Long> = Topic.of("customer.orders")
}
```

```java
public final class CustomerTopics {
    public static final Topic<String, Long> NAME = Topic.of("customer.name");
    public static final Topic<List<Order>, Long> ORDERS = Topic.of("customer.orders");

    private CustomerTopics() {}
}
```

## 2. Subscribe in a view

```kotlin
class CustomerOrdersView(
    private val customerId: Long,
    private val initialName: String,
    private val initialOrders: List<Order>,
) : Component() {

    private val name = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName)
    private val orders = topic(CustomerTopics.ORDERS, customerId, initialOrders)

    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8) {
        Text(name)                          // Signal<String>
        ForEach(orders) { OrderCard(it) }   // Signal<List<Order>>
    }
}
```

`topic(...)` returns a regular `Signal<T>`, so `Text(signal)`,
`ForEach(signal)`, `signal.map { }`, and `computed { }` all work. Subscribing is
idempotent per `(topic, subject)` within a session; repeated calls return the
same local signal.

Passing the wrong subject or payload type is a compile error: `NAME` requires a
`Long` subject and a `String` value.

## 3. Publish from any thread

The starter produces a `PathlandSignalHub` bean for the root mount (use
`PathlandHost.signalHub(mount)` in a multi-app host). Publishing is
non-blocking.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class CustomerConsumers {

    @Inject PathlandSignalHub hub;

    @Incoming("customer-name-changed")
    void onNameChanged(CustomerNameChanged event) {
        hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, event.customerId(), event.name());
    }
}
```

Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
touches customer 43.

## Global topics

Some signals are app-wide rather than per-entity (a feature flag, a global
counter, a service-status banner). Declare those with `Topic.global`:

```kotlin
object AppTopics {
    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed")
}
```

```kotlin
// subscribe (every session that renders this line)
val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)
Text(computed { "Events consumed: ${events.get()}" })
```

```java
// publish (any thread)
hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
```

A global topic is still subscription-targeted: only sessions that called
`topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, …)` update. A session that never subscribed is
untouched. There is deliberately no "publish to every subject" operation.

The two-argument `topic(...)`/`publish(...)` overloads only accept
`Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so a scoped topic cannot be published globally and a
global topic cannot be published with a customer/order id. `GlobalSubject` is
reserved as an application subject.

## Semantics

- **Scoped, not broadcast.** The hub looks up subscribers by
  `(topic.name, subject)`. An unscoped global topic uses the singleton
  `GlobalSubject` as its subject, so it reaches only the sessions that
  subscribed to that topic — never every live session. There is no
  publish-to-all-subjects path.
- **Actor-confined.** Published values are applied on the session actor, so all
  signal reads/writes/effects keep the single-threaded contract.
- **Latest wins.** Publishes are coalesced per session: at most one drain task is
  scheduled, and only the newest value per subscription is applied. A hot
  producer cannot flood the actor.
- **`initial` seeds the signal.** A new session renders current data from its own
  source; subsequent changes arrive through `publish`. Late subscribers do not
  receive historical values.
- **Session-scoped lifetime.** Subscriptions end when the session closes.
  `SessionContext.current()?.unsubscribe(topic, subject)` is available for dynamic
  subjects; SSR sessions subscribe for the first paint but do not register with
  the hub.
- **Multi-app isolation.** Each mounted app has its own hub; `/` and `/billing`
  never see each other's topics.

## Notes

- Declare a topic once and share the constant. The topic name is the wire
  identity (a future Redis fan-out can route on it); two topics with the same
  name must carry the same types.
- The subject should be immutable with stable `equals`/`hashCode` — an id, a
  value class, or a record.
- For an app-wide stream, use an explicit singleton subject
  (`object GlobalSubject`) as the `S` type; every subscription is still scoped.
- If you need a lower-level escape hatch, `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` and
  `SessionContext.current()?.submit { }` run work on the session actor.
